12.2 Big Bang theory and Hubble's study
12.3 Future of the universe: open, flat and closed universe and Big Crunch

html:
On a clear night in the hills of Nepal, you can see thousands of stars and a pale band of light across the sky, the Milky Way. People have watched the sky for thousands of years and asked: what are the stars? How did everything begin?

Are we alone? In this unit you will learn about the stars, galaxies and the solar system, the Big Bang theory of how the universe began, and how humans explore space with telescopes, satellites, rockets and probes.

What SEE asks from this unit

Expect: the importance of gravitational force in the universe (2 marks); the Big Bang theory and Hubble's study / Hubble's law (v = Hd) with its velocity–distance graph and redshift (2–4 marks); critical density and the future of the universe: open universe, flat universe, closed universe and Big Crunch with the size-vs-time graph (2–4 marks); and short questions on light year, astronomical unit, stars, galaxies and satellites.

12.1 Universe and the importance of gravitational force

Importance of gravitational force in the universe

Although gravitational force is the weakest of the four fundamental forces of nature, it acts over infinite distances and is always attractive. Therefore, gravitational force is the master force that shapes the structure, stability and evolution of the entire universe:

  1. Birth of stars and galaxies: Gravity pulls vast clouds of hydrogen and helium gas and cosmic dust (nebulae) together, compressing and heating their cores until nuclear fusion ignites and stars and galaxies are born.
  2. Orbital stability of solar and planetary systems: The Sun's gravitational pull keeps the eight planets, dwarf planets, asteroids and comets in stable elliptical orbits; likewise, planetary gravity holds natural moons and artificial satellites in orbit.
  3. Large-scale cosmic structure: Gravity binds billions of stars into galaxies (such as the Milky Way) and holds thousands of galaxies together in galaxy clusters and superclusters, preventing celestial bodies from scattering into empty space.
  4. Life-sustaining conditions on Earth: Earth's gravity retains the atmosphere and hydrosphere (oceans) around the planet, drives rainfall, snowfall and river flow, and together with the Moon's and Sun's gravity produces ocean tides.
  5. Determining the future fate of the universe: The inward pull of gravity of all matter in the cosmos opposes the outward expansion of the universe; whether the universe expands forever (open/flat universe) or collapses back (closed universe / Big Crunch) depends on the strength of gravitational attraction relative to the expansion rate.

The universe and its size

Universe

The universe is everything that exists: all matter, energy, space and time, including the stars, planets, galaxies and everything in between.

The universe is so large that kilometres are too small to measure it. Astronomers use two bigger units.

  • Astronomical unit (AU): the average distance from the Earth to the Sun, about 1.5\times10^{8} km. Used inside the solar system.
  • Light year (ly): the distance travelled by light in one year in vacuum. Used for stars and galaxies.

1\ \text{ly} = 3\times10^{5}\ \text{km s}^{-1} \times 3.15\times10^{7}\ \text{s} \approx 9.46\times10^{12}\ \text{km}

A light year is a distance

The "year" in light year can mislead. A light year measures distance, not time. Light from a star 10 light years away takes 10 years to reach us.

Light travel time

Problem. The Sun is 1.5\times10^{8} km from the Earth. How long does sunlight take to reach the Earth? (Speed of light = 3\times10^{5} km s⁻¹.)

Solution. t = \dfrac{d}{v} = \dfrac{1.5\times10^{8}}{3\times10^{5}} = 500 s = 8 min 20 s.

So we see the Sun as it was about 8 minutes ago.

Distance of a star

Problem. The nearest star after the Sun, Proxima Centauri, is 4.24 light years away. Express this distance in kilometres.

Solution. d = 4.24 \times 9.46\times10^{12} = 4.0\times10^{13} km.

Even the nearest star is about 40 trillion kilometres away.

Stars

Star

A star is a huge, hot, glowing ball of gas (mostly hydrogen and helium) that produces its own heat and light by nuclear fusion in its core.

In the core of a star, the temperature is millions of degrees. Hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium and a vast amount of energy is released (nuclear fusion).

The outward push of this energy balances the inward pull of gravity, so the star stays stable for billions of years.

  • Our nearest star is the Sun. It is a medium-sized yellow star about 4.6 billion years old, and is expected to shine for about another 5 billion years.
  • Stars twinkle because their light passes through the moving layers of the Earth's atmosphere and is refracted differently from moment to moment. Planets are nearer and look like tiny discs, so they do not twinkle much.
  • The colour of a star shows its surface temperature: blue-white stars are the hottest, yellow (like the Sun) are medium, red stars are cooler.
  • Stars differ in size, from tiny neutron stars to supergiants hundreds of times the Sun's diameter, and in brightness.

Life cycle of a star

A star is born, lives and dies. The path depends on its mass.

  1. Nebula. A huge cloud of gas (hydrogen) and dust.
  2. Protostar. Gravity pulls the cloud together; it becomes denser and hotter.
  3. Main-sequence star. Hydrogen fusion begins in the core; the star shines steadily for most of its life (about 10 billion years for the Sun).
  4. Red giant (or red supergiant). When hydrogen in the core runs out, the star swells and cools on the outside.
  5. Death. - A star like the Sun throws off its outer layers (a planetary nebula) and the core shrinks into a white dwarf, which cools slowly into a black dwarf. - A star much heavier than the Sun (about 8 or more solar masses) ends in a violent explosion called a supernova. The core then becomes a neutron star, or, if the star was very heavy, a black hole.

Time on the main sequence

Problem. The Sun is about 4.6 billion years old and will live about 10 billion years in total on the main sequence. How much longer will it shine as a main-sequence star?

Solution. Remaining life \approx 10 - 4.6 = 5.4 billion years, or roughly 5 billion years.

Constellations

A constellation is a group of stars that looks like a pattern in the sky. The stars in a constellation are not close together; they only appear so as we look from Earth. There are 88 official constellations.

  • Ursa Major (Great Bear, Saptarshi): seven bright stars forming a ladle or plough. Two of its stars, the "pointers", point toward the Pole Star.
  • Orion (Mrigashira): a hunter with three stars in a row as his belt; seen in the winter sky.
  • Cassiopeia: a W-shaped group.
  • Pole Star (Polaris, Dhruva Tara): appears almost fixed in the northern sky, because it lies almost exactly above the Earth's axis of rotation. Travellers once used it for finding north.

All stars appear to move from east to west during the night because the Earth spins from west to east.

Galaxies

Galaxy

A galaxy is a huge system of billions of stars, gas, dust and dark matter, held together by gravity.

There are hundreds of billions of galaxies in the observable universe. Galaxies are classified by shape:

Type Shape Example
Spiral Flat rotating disc with spiral arms and a central bulge Milky Way, Andromeda
Elliptical Round or oval ball of old stars M87
Irregular No definite shape Large and Small Magellanic Clouds

The Milky Way is our home galaxy: a spiral galaxy about 100,000 light years across with at least 100 billion stars.

Our Sun lies in one of its arms, about 26,000 light years from the centre, and takes about 230 million years to go once around it. From the Earth we see the Milky Way edge-on as a band of light across the sky.

The nearest large galaxy is Andromeda, about 2.5 million light years away.

The solar system

Solar system

The solar system is the Sun together with all the bodies that move around it: eight planets, their moons, dwarf planets, asteroids, comets and meteoroids.

The Sun contains more than 99 % of the mass of the solar system, and its gravity holds everything in orbit. The solar system is about 4.6 billion years old.

The planets in order from the Sun: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.

Remember the order

My Very Educated Mother Just Served Us Noodles.

Planet Distance from Sun (AU) Diameter (km) Time for one revolution Moons Notes
Mercury 0.39 4,879 88 days 0 Smallest planet; nearest to the Sun
Venus 0.72 12,104 225 days 0 Hottest planet (about 460 °C, thick CO₂ atmosphere); spins backwards
Earth 1.00 12,742 365.25 days 1 Only known planet with life
Mars 1.52 6,779 687 days 2 "Red planet" (iron oxide); Olympus Mons is the biggest volcano
Jupiter 5.20 139,820 11.9 years many (90+) Largest planet; Great Red Spot storm
Saturn 9.58 116,460 29.5 years many (140+) Bright rings of ice; less dense than water
Uranus 19.2 50,724 84 years 28 Rotates on its side; blue-green (methane)
Neptune 30.1 49,244 165 years 16 Farthest planet; windy and cold

The first four (Mercury to Mars) are the inner (terrestrial) planets: small, rocky and dense. Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune are the outer (giant) planets: very large, made mostly of gas and ice, and having rings.

Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants; Uranus and Neptune are ice giants.

Kepler's third law. For planets orbiting the Sun, the square of the time of one revolution is proportional to the cube of the average distance from the Sun: T^2 \propto r^3. If T is in years and r in AU, then T^2 = r^3.

Using Kepler's third law

Problem. A planet orbits the Sun at an average distance of 4 AU. Find its time period.

Solution. T^2 = r^3 = 4^3 = 64, so T = 8 years.

Dwarf planets. In 2006 the International Astronomical Union defined a planet as a body that orbits the Sun, is round, and has cleared its orbit of other bodies. Pluto does not clear its orbit, so it is a dwarf planet, as are Ceres, Eris, Haumea and Makemake.

Moon. The Moon is the Earth's only natural satellite. Its diameter is about one quarter of the Earth's, and it is about 384,000 km away. It takes about 27.3 days to orbit the Earth and shows the same face to us always.

It has no air or water, so the daytime is hot (about 127 °C) and the night is very cold (about −173 °C). Its gravity is one sixth of the Earth's.

The phases of the Moon (new moon to full moon) arise because we see different portions of the lit half as the Moon goes round the Earth. Tides in the sea are caused mainly by the Moon's gravity.

Eclipses. A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon comes between the Sun and the Earth (on a new moon day) and its shadow falls on the Earth.

A lunar eclipse occurs when the Earth comes between the Sun and the Moon (on a full moon day) and the Moon moves into the Earth's shadow.

We do not get an eclipse every month because the Moon's orbit is tilted by about 5° to the Earth's orbit.

Other members.

Body What it is
Asteroids Rocky lumps, mostly in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter
Comets Balls of ice, dust and rock in long orbits. Near the Sun they develop a glowing head and a tail pointing away from the Sun. Halley's comet returns about every 76 years
Meteoroids Small rocky pieces in space
Meteors ("shooting stars") Meteoroids burning up as they enter the Earth's atmosphere
Meteorites Meteors that reach the ground

12.2 Big Bang theory and Hubble's study

The Big Bang theory

The most widely accepted explanation for the origin of the universe is the Big Bang theory.

Big Bang theory

According to the Big Bang theory, the universe began about 13.8 billion years ago from an extremely hot and dense point, which expanded rapidly in a huge explosion-like event. The universe has been expanding and cooling ever since.

It is not an explosion in space; it is the expansion of space itself. A useful picture is a balloon with dots drawn on it. As the balloon is blown up, every dot moves away from every other dot, and no dot is the centre.

Main stages:

  1. Beginning (time zero): all matter and energy are packed in a tiny, hot, dense state.
  2. First fraction of a second: rapid expansion; fundamental particles (quarks, electrons) form.
  3. First few minutes: protons and neutrons join to form the nuclei of hydrogen and helium.
  4. About 380,000 years: the universe has cooled enough for atoms to form; light is free to travel. This relic light is still seen today as the cosmic microwave background.
  5. After a few hundred million years: gravity pulls gas together to form the first stars and galaxies.
  6. About 9 billion years after the Big Bang (4.6 billion years ago): our Sun and solar system form from a cloud of gas and dust.

Hubble's Study and Hubble's Law

In 1929 the American astronomer Edwin Hubble analysed the spectra of light coming from distant galaxies using the Mount Wilson telescope and made two landmark discoveries:

  1. Redshift of galactic light: The spectral lines of light from distant galaxies are shifted towards the longer-wavelength red end of the visible spectrum (Doppler redshift), proving that galaxies are moving away from us and from one another in every direction.
  2. Hubble's Law: The farther a galaxy is from the observer, the faster it recedes.
Hubble's Law

Hubble's law states that the recession velocity (v) of a distant galaxy moving away from us is directly proportional to its distance (d) from us:

v \propto d \quad \Longrightarrow \quad v = H d

where H (or H_0) is the Hubble constant (H \approx 70\text{–}73.8\ \text{km s}^{-1}\text{Mpc}^{-1}; 1\ \text{Mpc} \approx 3.26 \times 10^6\ \text{light years}).

  • Significance of Hubble's law and the v vs d graph:
  • Plotting recession velocity (v) on the y-axis against distance (d) on the x-axis gives a straight line passing through the origin, whose slope equals the Hubble constant (H = v/d).
  • Because H has dimensions of 1/\text{time}, the reciprocal 1/H estimates the age of the universe (\approx 13.8\ \text{billion years}).
  • It provides the strongest observational proof of the expanding universe and the Big Bang theory.
  • Other evidence for the Big Bang: (i) Cosmic Microwave Background Radiation (CMBR) at 2.7\ \text{K} discovered by Penzias and Wilson (1965), the cooled afterglow of the early universe; (ii) primordial abundance of about 75\% hydrogen and 25\% helium by mass.
Recession speed of a galaxy (Hubble's law)

Problem. A galaxy is at a distance of 100\ \text{Mpc} (megaparsecs). Using H = 70\ \text{km s}^{-1}\text{Mpc}^{-1}, find the velocity with which it recedes from us. What happens to its recession velocity if another galaxy is twice as far (200\ \text{Mpc})?

Solution. By Hubble's law, v = H d = 70 \times 100 = 7000\ \text{km s}^{-1}. For a galaxy at 200\ \text{Mpc}, the recession velocity doubles to v = 70 \times 200 = 14000\ \text{km s}^{-1}.

12.3 Future of the universe: open, flat and closed universe and Big Crunch

Critical Density (\rho_c) and the Three Models of the Future Universe

While the momentum of the Big Bang makes galaxies fly apart, the gravitational attraction of all matter in the universe pulls them inward and slows the expansion.

The ultimate fate of the universe depends on how the actual average density of the universe (\rho) compares with a threshold value called the critical density (\rho_c).

Critical density

Critical density (\rho_c) is the exact average mass density of the universe Required for gravitational attraction to just balance the outward expansion so that the expansion gradually slows toward zero without ever re-collapsing. Its estimated value is:

\rho_c = \frac{3H^2}{8\pi G} \approx (1\text{ to }3) \times 10^{-26}\ \text{kg m}^{-3}

(roughly 3\text{ to }6 hydrogen atoms per cubic metre of space).

Model of Universe Density Condition Curvature of Space Future Fate of the Universe
1. Open Universe Actual density is less than critical density (\rho < \rho_c) Negatively curved (saddle-shaped / hyperbolic) Gravity is too weak to halt expansion; the universe keeps expanding forever at a steady/accelerating rate, eventually cooling into a Big Freeze / Cold Death
2. Flat Universe Actual density equals critical density (\rho = \rho_c) Zero curvature (flat Euclidean geometry) Gravity exactly balances expansion; the expansion slows down continuously and approaches zero speed only at infinite time, never re-collapsing
3. Closed Universe Actual density is greater than critical density (\rho > \rho_c) Positively curved (spherical, finite volume) Strong gravity eventually stops the expansion and pulls all galaxies back together into a single super-hot, super-dense point (singularity) in an event called the Big Crunch
Big Crunch

If the average density of the universe exceeds the critical density (\rho > \rho_c), gravitational pull eventually halts the outward expansion of galaxies and reverses it into a cosmic contraction, collapsing all matter and space back into a single hot, dense singularity.

This hypothetical end of a closed universe is called the Big Crunch (which some oscillating-universe models suggest could be followed by another Big Bang).

Space exploration and artificial satellites

Why explore space?

To understand the origin and future of the universe, to find life elsewhere, to find new resources, to improve life on Earth with new technologies (weather forecasting, communication, GPS, medical imaging), and to study threats such as asteroids.

Tools of space exploration

Telescopes. Optical telescopes collect visible light. Radio telescopes collect radio waves from space (Jodrell Bank, Arecibo).

Space telescopes avoid the blurring and absorption of the atmosphere: the Hubble Space Telescope (1990) and the James Webb Space Telescope (launched 2021, infrared) have shown galaxies at enormous distances.

Rockets. A rocket works on Newton's third law: hot gas is thrown out backward at high speed, and the rocket moves forward with an equal momentum. To reach orbit, the rocket must reach about 8 km s⁻¹.

Rockets are built in stages; each stage is dropped when its fuel is used up so that the remaining rocket is lighter.

Speed needed to leave the Earth

Problem. An object must have a speed called the escape velocity v = \sqrt{2gR} to leave the Earth for ever. Find it for g = 9.8 m s⁻² and R = 6.4\times10^{6} m.

Solution. v = \sqrt{2 \times 9.8 \times 6.4\times10^{6}} = \sqrt{1.254\times10^{8}} = 1.12\times10^{4} m s⁻¹ = 11.2 km s⁻¹.

(The speed needed to stay in a low orbit is smaller, \sqrt{gR} \approx 7.9 km s⁻¹.)

Artificial satellites

An artificial satellite is a man-made object that revolves around the Earth (or another body). It stays in orbit because the gravitational pull supplies the force needed to keep it moving in a circle; it is in a continuous free fall around the Earth.

Type Height Period Uses
Low Earth orbit (LEO) 200–2,000 km about 90 min Earth observation, International Space Station, spy and remote-sensing satellites
Polar orbit about 800 km about 100 min Map-making, weather, covers the whole Earth as it turns below
Geostationary orbit 36,000 km above the equator 24 h Communication, TV broadcast, weather. It stays above the same point on the Earth

A geostationary satellite revolves from west to east with the same period as the Earth's rotation (24 h), so it always appears fixed over one point of the sky.

Uses of satellites: communication (telephone, TV, internet), weather forecasting, navigation (GPS), remote sensing (forests, glaciers, floods, land use), military surveillance, and scientific research.

Nepal in space. In 2019 Nepal sent its first satellite, NepaliSat-1, a small cube about 10 cm on a side built by Nepali engineers in Japan as part of the BIRDS-3 project.

It was launched to the International Space Station and released into orbit to take images of Nepal's land and mountains. Nepal also uses foreign satellites for weather and remote sensing, e.g. monitoring glaciers and glacial lakes.

Milestones of space exploration

Year Event
1957 USSR launches Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite (4 October). Dog Laika orbits in Sputnik 2
1961 Yuri Gagarin (USSR) becomes the first human in space (12 April)
1963 Valentina Tereshkova, first woman in space
1969 Apollo 11 (USA): Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walk on the Moon (20 July)
1977 Voyager 1 and 2 launched; Voyager 1 later entered interstellar space
1981–2011 Space Shuttle flights
1990 Hubble Space Telescope launched
1998 First part of the International Space Station (ISS) launched
2008 India's Chandrayaan-1 finds evidence of water on the Moon
2021 NASA's Perseverance rover lands on Mars; James Webb Space Telescope launched
2023 Chandrayaan-3 (India) lands near the Moon's south pole

Space stations, probes and rovers

  • Space station. The International Space Station is a large laboratory orbiting about 400 km above the Earth, built and run by the USA, Russia, Europe, Japan and Canada. Astronauts live there for months and carry out experiments in weightlessness.
  • Space probes are unmanned spacecraft sent to study planets and other bodies from near or far: Voyager, Cassini (Saturn), New Horizons (Pluto).
  • Rovers are vehicles that drive on another world: Curiosity and Perseverance on Mars.

Problems and dangers

  • Space debris. Thousands of broken satellites and pieces of rocket orbit the Earth at high speed and can damage working satellites.
  • Cost and risk to human life; harmful radiation and weightlessness (muscle and bone loss).
  • Pollution of the upper atmosphere from rocket launches.
Writing about satellites

When asked to "explain how a geostationary satellite is useful", give: orbit at 36,000 km above the equator, period 24 h, appears fixed in the sky, therefore a single dish antenna on the ground can keep pointing at it for TV and communication.

Chapter summary

  • Gravitational force forms stars from nebulae, binds stars into galaxies and galaxy clusters, keeps planets and satellites in orbit, retains Earth's atmosphere/hydrosphere, and governs the future fate of the universe.
  • The universe is everything that exists. 1\ \text{light year} = 9.46\times10^{12}\ \text{km} (distance); 1\ \text{AU} = 1.5\times10^{8}\ \text{km}.
  • Big Bang theory: The universe began about 13.8\ \text{billion years} ago from an extremely hot, dense singularity and has been expanding and cooling ever since.
  • Hubble's law: The recession velocity (v) of a distant galaxy is directly proportional to its distance (d): v = Hd, where H \approx 70\text{–}73.8\ \text{km s}^{-1}\text{Mpc}^{-1} is the Hubble constant. Spectral redshift proves galaxies are moving apart.
  • Critical density (\rho_c \approx (1\text{–}3)\times 10^{-26}\ \text{kg m}^{-3}): The boundary density at which gravity just balances expansion.
  • Future of the universe: Open universe (\rho < \rho_c) expands forever; Flat universe (\rho = \rho_c) expands at a decreasing rate approaching zero at infinity; Closed universe (\rho > \rho_c) stops expanding and contracts back into a singularity (Big Crunch).
  • Satellites stay in orbit because gravity supplies the centripetal force. Geostationary satellites orbit at 36,000\ \text{km} with a 24\ \text{h} period; NepaliSat-1 (2019) was Nepal's first satellite.

Practice questions

Group A — Objective (1 mark each)

  1. A light year is a unit of [1]atimebdistancecspeeddbrightness
  2. The planet nearest to the Sun is [1]aVenusbMarscMercurydEarth
  3. The most accepted theory of the origin of the universe is the [1]aSteady State theorybBig Bang theorycNebular theory onlydPulsating theory
  4. The star at the end of a Sun-like star's life is a [1]ablack holebneutron starcwhite dwarfdsupernova
  5. A geostationary satellite has a period of [1]a90 minutesb12 hoursc24 hoursd365 days
Answers to Group A

1. (b) — it is the distance light travels in a year.

2. (c) — Mercury is 0.39 AU from the Sun.

3. (b) — supported by red shift and the microwave background.

4. (c) — a Sun-like star sheds its outer layers and leaves a white dwarf.

5. (c) — it matches the Earth's rotation, so it stays above one spot.

Group B — Short answer (2 marks each)

  1. Define a light year. How long does light from the Sun take to reach the Earth? [2]
  2. Why do stars twinkle but planets do not? [2]
  3. Name the types of galaxy. To which type does the Milky Way belong? [2]
  4. Why is Pluto not called a planet? [2]
  5. Give any two uses of artificial satellites. [2]
Answers to Group B

1. A light year is the distance travelled by light in one year in vacuum (9.46\times10^{12} km). Sunlight takes about 8 min 20 s (500 s).

2. The light of stars is refracted by the moving layers of the atmosphere, so its apparent position and brightness keep changing. Planets are nearer and look like small discs; the changes from different points average out.

3. Spiral, elliptical and irregular. The Milky Way is a spiral galaxy.

4. Pluto has not cleared its orbit of other bodies, so in 2006 it was classified as a dwarf planet.

5. Any two: communication, weather forecasting, navigation (GPS), remote sensing, TV broadcast.

Group C — Long answer (4 marks each)

  1. Describe the life cycle of a star like the Sun and of a massive star. [4]
  2. State the Big Bang theory and give two pieces of evidence for it. [4]
  3. A star is 8.6 light years away. Find its distance in kilometres and the time light from it takes to reach us. [4]
  4. State Hubble's law and write its mathematical formula. How does Hubble's study support the Big Bang theory? [4]
  5. What is critical density? Explain the open, flat and closed models of the future universe and define the Big Crunch with a diagram. [4]
  6. Write any four points showing the importance of gravitational force in the universe. [4]
Answers to Group C

1. Sun-like: nebula → protostar → main sequence → red giant → planetary nebula → white dwarf. Massive: nebula → protostar → main sequence → red supergiant → supernova → neutron star or black hole.

2. Statement: the universe began about 13.8 billion years ago from a hot, dense state and has been expanding. Evidence: red shift of distant galaxies (they recede, faster if farther); cosmic microwave background of 2.7 K; abundance of hydrogen and helium.

3. d = 8.6 \times 9.46\times10^{12} = 8.14\times10^{13} km. Time = 8.6 years.

4. Hubble's law: The recession velocity (v) of a distant galaxy is directly proportional to its distance (d) from us: v = Hd, where H is the Hubble constant. Hubble observed that light from distant galaxies is redshifted, proving that all galaxies are moving away from one another; reversing this expansion in time shows that all matter was once concentrated at a single point, strongly supporting the Big Bang theory.

5. Critical density (\rho_c \approx (1\text{–}3)\times 10^{-26}\ \text{kg m}^{-3}) is the average cosmic density at which gravity just balances expansion. (i) Open universe (\rho < \rho_c): gravity is too weak, so the universe expands forever; (ii) Flat universe (\rho = \rho_c): expansion slows and approaches zero velocity at infinity; (iii) Closed universe (\rho > \rho_c): strong gravity stops expansion and pulls all galaxies back into a single hot, dense singularity called the Big Crunch. (Draw Figure 2b.)

6. Gravitational force: (i) compresses nebulae to form stars and galaxies; (ii) keeps planets, moons and satellites in stable orbits; (iii) binds stars into galaxies and galaxy clusters; (iv) retains Earth's atmosphere and oceans and determines whether the universe will expand forever or re-collapse.

Group D — Model answers for long questions (10 marks each, for deeper revision)

  1. Describe the Big Bang theory and the evidence supporting it. [10]
  2. Describe the solar system, with a table of its planets. Explain the life cycle of a star and the future of the Sun. [10]

Model answer D1: the Big Bang theory (10 marks)

Introduction. The universe is everything that exists: all matter, energy, space and time. It contains about two trillion galaxies, and our galaxy, the Milky Way, has over 100 billion stars. The most accepted theory about its origin is the Big Bang theory.

The theory. About 13.8 billion years ago, all matter and energy were packed in an extremely hot and dense point. It suddenly began to expand, and space itself started stretching. This was not an explosion in space; it was an expansion of space.

Stages in the history of the universe.

  1. The first second. The universe was hotter than billions of degrees. Matter and energy were mixed. It expanded very quickly.
  2. After some minutes. Protons and neutrons joined to form nuclei of hydrogen and helium.
  3. After about 380,000 years. The universe cooled to about 3,000 K. Electrons joined with nuclei to form atoms, and light could travel freely. This light is still around us.
  4. After hundreds of millions of years. Gravity pulled gas clouds together to form the first stars and galaxies.
  5. After about 9 billion years. Our Sun and the solar system formed, around 4.6 billion years ago.

Evidence for the theory.

Evidence Meaning
Expansion of the universe (Hubble, 1929): distant galaxies move away and the farther they are, the faster they go If the galaxies were closer in the past, everything began from one point
Red shift: light from distant galaxies is shifted toward red Shows the galaxies are receding
Cosmic microwave background radiation (CMBR): weak microwaves from all directions at 2.7 K The leftover glow of the hot early universe
Abundance of light elements: about 75% hydrogen and 25% helium Matches the prediction of the early hot universe

Fate and other ideas. The universe may continue to expand for ever (Big Freeze), or gravity may stop it and pull it back together (Big Crunch). Present observations show the expansion is speeding up due to dark energy.

Conclusion. The Big Bang theory is supported by strong observational evidence, and the Hubble Ultra Deep Field shows young galaxies billions of years old.

Model answer D2: the solar system and the life of a star (10 marks)

Introduction. The solar system is the Sun and all objects bound to it by gravity: eight planets, their moons, dwarf planets, asteroids, comets and meteoroids. The Sun contains 99.8 percent of its mass.

Planet Type Moons Notes
Mercury Rocky 0 Nearest to the Sun, no atmosphere
Venus Rocky 0 Hottest planet (about 460 °C), thick CO₂
Earth Rocky 1 Only known planet with life
Mars Rocky 2 Red, polar ice caps, rovers search for past life
Jupiter Gas giant Many Largest, Great Red Spot
Saturn Gas giant Many Bright rings
Uranus Ice giant Many Rotates on its side
Neptune Ice giant Many Farthest, strong winds

The asteroid belt lies between Mars and Jupiter. Comets are balls of ice and dust with a tail that grows when they come close to the Sun, as Halley's comet does every 76 years.

Life cycle of a star.

  1. Nebula: a huge cloud of gas (hydrogen) and dust.
  2. Protostar: gravity pulls the cloud together and it heats up.
  3. Main-sequence star: hydrogen fuses into helium and gives out energy. The Sun is in this stage and will stay for about 10 billion years in total.
  4. Red giant: when the hydrogen is used up, the star swells and cools.
  5. Fate depends on mass.
Mass of star End
Small or medium (like the Sun) Sheds outer layers (planetary nebula), the core becomes a white dwarf, and finally cools to a black dwarf
Large Red supergiant, explodes as a supernova, leaves a neutron star
Very large Supernova, the core collapses to a black hole

Future of the Sun. In about 5 billion years the Sun will become a red giant, then a white dwarf.

Space exploration. Telescopes, satellites, probes (Voyager), rovers on Mars, and space stations like the ISS have increased our knowledge. Nepal's first satellites, NepaliSat-1 and the Munal satellite, were built by Nepali engineers and launched in 2019 and 2020.

Conclusion. The solar system is one small part of the Milky Way, and stars are born, live and die according to their mass.
